title: Word equations with linear length constraints
formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine which halts on every input consisting of a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\), a finite system of word equations \(U_i=V_i\) and a finite conjunction of integer linear equalities and inequalities on variable lengths, and answers YES exactly when they admit a simultaneous solution in the free monoid \(\Sigma^*\)? The alphabet, equations, variables and arithmetic coefficients are all part of the input. No bound on the running time is prescribed.
definitions: The alphabet \(\Sigma\) is a finite nonempty set of constant letters. The finite set of variables \(X=\{X_1,\ldots,X_k\}\) is disjoint from \(\Sigma\); \(k\) may be zero. Each side \(U_i,V_i\) is an explicitly written finite word over \(\Sigma\cup X\), including the empty word. A substitution \(\sigma:X\to\Sigma^*\) assigns one finite word to each variable and extends by concatenation while fixing each constant letter. Every occurrence of a variable receives the same word, and empty substitutions are allowed. Each equation requires literal equality \(\sigma(U_i)=\sigma(V_i)\). The length \(|w|\) of a word is its number of letters. Each arithmetic atom has the form \(\sum_{j=1}^{k}a_j|\sigma(X_j)|\le b\) or \(\sum_{j=1}^{k}a_j|\sigma(X_j)|=b\), with signed binary integer coefficients and constants. Every supplied atom must hold for the same substitution as every equation. Empty lists of equations or constraints are allowed and mean the empty conjunction. Alphabet and variable symbols have finite identifiers; equation sides are explicit lists and arithmetic atoms are explicit coefficient lists. Nothing is given as a circuit or a compressed word. The machine is one uniform program over all input sizes, alphabet sizes, variable counts, equation counts and coefficient values; it halts on both positive and negative instances. Malformed inputs may be rejected. Only existential choice of the substituted words is involved. There is no variable-times-variable product of lengths, individual-letter count, regular-language predicate, string-to-integer conversion or universal string quantifier. Nonempty-variable requirements are expressible by \(-|\sigma(X_j)|\le-1\), but they are not imposed unless present in the input. This is exact satisfiability, with no random error, oracle, numerical tolerance or complexity bound.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean proof that a total computable YES/NO procedure exists for exactly the encoded input class above, or that no such procedure exists. A positive answer must verify termination on every input and equivalence of YES with existence of one simultaneous substitution satisfying all word and arithmetic constraints. It need not output a substitution or satisfy a time bound. A negative answer must prove noncomputability for this length-only existential conjunction problem; a result using extra predicates, stronger quantification, or a failure of one particular procedure does not suffice. Acceptance is exact and has no numerical tolerance. This editorial audit does not supply a Lean formalization.
why: A fundamental boundary for reasoning about concatenation and numerical size simultaneously. It governs whether a complete terminating solver can exist for a basic fragment of string constraints used in verification, while connecting free-monoid equations, arithmetic and reachability.

importance.reason: A longstanding decidability question at the intersection of formal languages, number-theoretic constraints and automated verification; even unrestricted termination is unknown, before asking for efficient algorithms.

progress.text: Makanin establishes decidability of plain word equations. Adding linear length constraints remains outside that theorem; the distinction is reviewed by Ciobanu.
Ciobanu’s survey explicitly separates the open length-constraint problem from undecidable letter-count and Parikh-image extensions.

Day and Konefal’s RP 2025 paper appears online, giving decidability for quadratic equations with at most two unknowns and semilinear constraints on solution lengths. The proceedings carry a 2026 copyright year.
Version 3 of Barros, Cadilhac, and Pérez claims NEXP-hardness for the nonerasing positive-Boolean formulation. Only its arithmetic-with-divisibility problem is asserted NEXP-complete.
Przybocki and Barrett’s IJCAR 2026 paper gives partial termination criteria for extended Nielsen transformations and explicitly retains general decidability as open.

Rechecked the original existential conjunction target, primary source models, restricted two-variable result, IJCAR termination theorem and July preprint’s separate Boolean/nonerasing lower-bound scope.

status_note: The checked DLT 2024 survey and IJCAR 2026 paper/full preprint explicitly retain unrestricted decidability as open. The RP 2025 theorem is limited to quadratic two-unknown equations. July 2026 preprint v3 claims NEXP-hardness of a nonerasing positive-Boolean formulation, not decidability or a matching complexity upper bound for the current conjunction problem. The 16 September 2026 audit verified these scopes and found no matching resolution in its bounded search.

context_blocks.text: The two ingredients are separately decidable: plain word equations by Makanin’s theorem and integer linear arithmetic by Presburger’s theorem. Their combination constrains both letter alignment and numerical size, and neither theorem alone settles their interaction.

Length identities can omit crucial content. For distinct letters \(a,b\), the word equation \(Xa=bX\) has no finite-word solution, although its induced length equality \(|X|+1=1+|X|\) is always satisfied. This illustrates why the target concerns a common word substitution, not merely a consistent length vector.

Restrictions on counts of individual letters, full Parikh vectors or additional quantifier alternation can yield different decidability results. Those predicates do not occur in the present input language. The distinction is explicit in Ciobanu’s survey.

Day and Konefal prove decidability for quadratic equations with at most two unknowns and semilinear constraints on their solution lengths. Quadratic means each unknown appears at most twice across the equation. Their RP 2025 paper appeared online in November 2025; its proceedings carry a 2026 copyright year. This restricted theorem does not cover an arbitrary system with unrestricted variable occurrences.

The IJCAR 2026 paper gives a sufficient termination condition and a partial converse for extended Nielsen transformations. The theorem concerns a specific procedure and a graph condition on an extended equation; it does not establish that every input of the unrestricted satisfiability problem is decidable. Its full preprint explicitly retains the general open question.

The checked July 2026 preprint states NEXP-hardness for nonerasing satisfiability of positive Boolean combinations of word equations and Presburger length constraints over two letters. Its NEXP-completeness theorem concerns existential arithmetic with divisibility. These are distinct claims, and neither is a decision procedure or an undecidability proof for the current card.

The saved target is a conjunction, while that lower-bound corollary permits disjunctions. Finite expansion relates their decidability questions, but need not preserve polynomial input size; the corollary is therefore not presented here as a checked NEXP lower bound for the exact conjunction encoding. Allowing empty substitutions is likewise kept distinct from the preprint’s nonerasing convention.

category_assignment.reason: The task solves simultaneous equations and arithmetic constraints on unknown strings.

sentences: Word equations require substitutions of finite strings that make all supplied concatenations identical.
Here the same substitution must also satisfy a conjunction of integer linear constraints on total string lengths.
The target is one always-terminating decision algorithm for arbitrary finite inputs, including empty substitutions and unrestricted variable occurrences.
Known restricted decision results and partial termination criteria do not settle this combination, and stronger letter-count predicates describe a different problem.
A resolution would establish whether complete exact solving is possible for this basic fragment of string constraints, before imposing efficiency requirements.
